04 · Read & review

The transcript

0:00 / 0:00

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

Emma was working at home when the newspaper archivist called. Staff had checked the old index again. They had found three entries about the student travel scheme in October 2011, including the one dated 12 October. The archivist warned that the index might be incomplete.

“Can you tell me what the other letters say?” Emma asked.

“Not yet. We can share the dates and general subjects, but not the private letters.”

One entry concerned questions about selection. Another was marked as a request for information. The third had the heading about a decision not received. The headings had been written by newspaper staff, not necessarily by the writers.

Emma copied the details into her notebook. Three entries did not mean three different families. One person could have written more than once, and some letters might never have been listed.

Sarah called while Emma was checking the dates.

“Three complaints,” Sarah said.

“Three index entries,” Emma corrected her. “We don't know whether all of them were complaints.”

Later Fiona Bell sent a short reply about the foundation's contact records. The records team had still not found any completed contact-attempt forms. They had found a page from an office guide explaining that staff should record letters returned by the post. Fiona could not confirm that every returned letter had been recorded.

“So we still don't know if any student missed a decision?” Emma asked.

“That's right. And I can't tell you whether the appeals folder contains any real appeals. It has not been checked.”

Emma thanked Fiona. She was disappointed, but she understood the limits of the evidence.

That afternoon she opened her notes from the interview with Claire in September 2011. Claire had worried about what the foundation promised and what students actually received. Emma remembered her own quick conclusion at the time. She had thought Claire simply disliked the foundation's directors.

Now she saw how much she had missed by not asking a better question.

Emma wrote four words across the page: Prepared. Sent. Received. Understood. A form could show the first stage. A register might show the second. But the last two needed information that the trust and the newspaper had not yet supplied.

Sarah sent a message: Can we publish something?

Emma replied: We can report what the documents say, but not a story about students losing their right to appeal. We don't have that evidence.

At the bottom of the archivist's email was one more detail: the three entries had been filed in different sections of the old index. Emma had assumed they were connected because they were about the same scheme. She decided to ask how those sections had been organised.

The answer might explain the entries—or show that she had put unrelated letters together.
